Representative_Docs: ["asking upperclassmen or alum: how was your gpa progression? ah yes this is a fun one. i'd say i definitely had an interesting gpa progression story looking back (i'm a senior graduating this december for context). so i dual enrolled at gt via distance math year 1 (basically taking math 1554 and 2551 during senior year of high school), and senioritis had the best of me let's just say. because gpa transfers if you're dual enrolling at the same school you'll attend for college, i actually started gt in fall 2019 with a 2.5 gpa on my record already (the lowest my cumulative has ever been). my first year gpa's were ok but not great, low 3's. then covid hit and the first two semesters were pretty good and my gpa was up to a 3.25 by the start of spring 2021. however, i had a really hard semester that included cs 3510, cs 2110 and ae 3030 in the same semester while starting ra-ing, and i ended up with a 2.6 semester gpa, which brought me down to a 3.1. since then, however, i'd say i've learned how to study more effectively (and i started using academic resources like tutoring, office hours, friends, etc.) and this past year i actually have been moving my gpa a decent bit (and honestly doing the best i've been at gt even w/ some of the hardest academic semesters i've ever faced - should be able to move it up to around a 3.3 overall by the end of this semester). case in point, it is definitely somewhat solidified as you go on, but if you have a great semester and improve study habits, your gpa can improve a decent bit. i think more importantly is that even when i had pretty trash gpa's like in spring 2021, i was still able to land my first internship. it's about learning, gaining skills, taking opportunities, and learning from your mistakes. i think that's more important than anything, everything else will fall in place. with all this said, i think with your situation as long as you improve study habits and take a reasonable load, you can definitely move it up to a 3.5, but even if not, it's not the end of the world! hope this long winded answer helped you :d", 'hey, bs/ms me here! i went through this last year so i know how it goes first off, if you’re graduating undergrad this semester, know that you can’t register for grad classes until phase ii registration, since you’re a “new” student again. that means that you’ll have plenty of time to figure out what’s available and what’s filled up. second, if you’re registering as an undergrad, you’ll need level permits to actually be able to register for grad classes. i believe that also opens during phase ii, so you can try to request overrides in advance but they may tell you to wait lastly, your actual question. i didn’t really struggle getting into any major area classes except for one, but it opened up within the first week of class. just like undergrad, people will drop classes within the first week of registration and you’ve got a decent chance of getting in. as an undergrad i went for me 6104 during my last semester and got in just fine by the way, not sure how you’re planning your grad school credit hours, but 9 credits in a semester is enough to fill up your time. i did 12 last semester and it took over time from my extra curriculars, so spread it out as much as you can', 'school difficulty with gatech? i know it\'s finals week (which may be felt in some of these posts), but as a gt alum (mgt 2000) this is giving me scary flashbacks. my son is currently at ksu (kennesaw state) but is transferring to gt starting summer term as having been offered and accepted a conditional transfer. i\'m excited for him, but i also know he\'s about to have academic culture shock coming from ksu. i\'ve followed his coursework enough at ksu and know enough about how things work at gt from experience and also from reading recent posts here, to know that there\'s a world of difference between the two (as illustrated in all the responses to this post). that said, for the folks who transferred in from ksu in engineering majors, what\'s your advice for a new transfer? my son will be a mechanical engineering major, so he\'s through calc 1, 2 and physics 1 (at ksu) and will start getting into the next classes (physics 2, etc.). i think he has to take linear algebra before multi-variable calculus; and still has to take cs 1371, me 1670 - so even though he\'s a "technically" sophomore by hours, he\'s a little behind where he would be if he had started at tech within his major. he\'s most likely only going to take one summer course (something "easy" and online - maybe apph 1040) because he has travel plans and can\'t really do the full summer term. then it\'s full time in the fall (and hopefully living on campus if he can get housing). he actually really enjoyed ksu (and to its credit, i do think it\'s a good school with good engineering programs), but he also felt like an opportunity to study engineering at georgia tech wasn\'t something to pass up. my advice was that #1 it\'s his decision - don\'t do it because you think it\'s what everyone else expects, but also #2 - people tend to regret the things they don\'t do (and not the things they do) - and i think he might regret not giving his best shot at gt, even knowing it will likely be overwhelming. worst case scenario, if it absolutely chews him up and he wants out, he could always go back to ksu. i just hope i didn\'t push him into something he\'s not ready for. again, looking for advice from the transfers out there... i want to see him succeed but also know you can\'t really express the challenges in words - you sort of have to live through it. i was a cs major before switching to management (now "business administration"), so i got a "taste" of the tough stuff before taking an easier path - but i knew i wanted to stay at georgia tech, so i figured out how to do it and keep my sanity. just saying that to recognize i know it\'s a lot tougher for engineering and computer science majors. sorry for the long post.']

Name: 0_cs_just_like_class
Representative_Docs: ["as a second year transfer student, i might completely fail my first semester here not exactly the same experience but i was more interested in getting drunk and laid than going to class when i first got to tech and almost failed out. realized real quick it wasn't just going to happen for me like high school did and something clicked. i made the decision i simply wasn't going to give up like a bunch of my peers did. just never quit. and after 5.5 years, it worked. and i'm so happy i did. no matter what else happens, no one can ever take that degree from you.", 'how to get into physics research as a transfer sophomore? letters from profs who don\'t do research are still fine for these positions. things like reus are competitive. while it is possible to get one without research experience, they do often look for some previous research skillset (not necessarily research. if you have coding experience, that is helpful). some of these positions do understand that students may not have opportunities (some physics departments don\'t have many professors or research), and so other rec letters are still helpful. if you transferred, you can get a rec letter from a prof at your previous college, or from a math or computer science course, etc. if you had a job, you could get a letter from your supervisor as well. however, not all research positions require rec letters. you can talk to professors in the department and ask if they are looking for students. i recommend getting involved in the physics groups in the department (sps, swip) which have older students active. for swip it is for anyone even though it is called the "society of women in physics" so there are also many faculty (of all genders) that go to meetings and you can learn about what they do and who may be willing to have an undergraduate student. after working for a bit, you and who you are working for may be able to apply for pura so you can get paid, but typically those applications get funded for students who have a good understanding of what they will be doing (so likely have worked a bit in the research group) and a mentor (grad student, postdoc, prof) willing to help them on the application.', "alumni, what was your starting salary exiting georgia tech? was it worth any debt you had? gt professor here- a lot of students focus on optimizing the $. instead, focus on optimizing your opportunities. in georgia tech computer science, plan for masters, not just bs. for ambitious students with the bsms program, it is possible to get your bs in 3-3.5 years. while doing that, do undergrad research for pay with the urop program to make yourself some $ and to make yourself valuable to a professor (or be an ugrad ta). apply for bsms and switch to ms as soon as you can. now your instate/outofstate tuition (plus a stipend to live on!) can be paid by being a teaching assistant or a graduate research assistant. (when you have impressed a professor or the teaching staff, be very clear about your intentions. almost all of us want to help students on their journey, but we can't read your mind! and we need at least a semester or two to arrange our finances to handle a new student.) once you have a good gra or gta job, slow down and spend at least 2 years in masters, absorbing everything you can. take the hard (and the fun!) classes. now you have had 5 years of education, have a masters in cs degree, and you have had enough experience with research/teaching to figure out if you want to do a phd (again, keep your professors informed on your goals). in cs, if you take advantage of the opportunities a top school offers, you debt burden is not going to be a problem (barring life changing events like accidents). top schools allow you to see (and be trained in) trends before industry hires for them. for example, four of my previous undergrads and masters who researched with me in wearable computers were hired for the apple vision pro\\ team (3 before it was announced). for what its worth, i have never personally focused on $; only opportunities. almost every job i have taken has been the lowest of the salaries offered but placed me with the smartest and most interesting co-workers. no regrets. good luck! \\personally, i prefer the minimalist approach of the vuzix z100."]

Name: 6_friends_people_clubs_feel
Representative_Docs: ['how to make friends when you’re shy?', "im happy i got into tech but sometimes i hate it here and i don't know what to do to improve my situation. yeah i feel you, i do not have any actual friends here myself and pretty much just do work and play games myself. while at this point i don’t care to make friends myself anymore while here for the moment, there are some things you can do. there is a discord directory for the school you could join and start talking to people with similar interests and plan to meet up. i think this is easier while being similar to a club as you can talk to people at the school. we also have a transfer discord thats somewhat active and chill, but most people don’t really meet up. the other thing people have said is to join clubs, but as someone who did this and had not good experiences, it is not going to be for everyone. most people in clubs are already friends with people in the clubs and it feels like they just hang out with their small group inside the club. basically, the only way to meet people here is by finding some sort of smaller niche group interest and then just talking to them in a club or online. there is probably some other stuff you could do but everything is going to require some amount of effort. gl and if you wanna talk more about stuff then just hmu.", 'am i the only one at gt without friends?']
